title: The Secret Cave
summary: Alone on Monte Cristo, Dantès follows Faria’s clues, blasts away a great rock, and makes his way through two hidden grottoes to Cardinal Spada’s chest, overflowing with gold coins, gold bars, and jewels.
details: Left behind by the smugglers after pretending to be injured, Dantès first climbs to the island’s highest point to make sure their ships have gone. He works out that the notches cut in the rocks lead to a hidden creek where Cardinal Spada could have landed in secret. A huge boulder puzzles him until he realizes it was never lifted into place: it was slid down a slope and wedged. Using the gunpowder his friend Jacopo left him, he blows out the wedge, levers the rock into the sea, and finds a flagstone with an iron ring, covering steps that lead underground.

Bracing himself for disappointment, he imagines that Cesare Borgia got there first, but goes down anyway with a wry “Perhaps!” The first grotto, lit through cracks in the rock, is empty. Remembering the words of the will, “in the farthest angle of the second opening,” he taps the walls, finds a patch of stucco painted to look like granite, and, after a moment when doubt nearly makes him faint, breaks through into a second, darker cave.

Digging in its corner, he strikes an oak chest bound with steel and engraved with the Spada coat of arms that Faria had so often drawn for him. He forces it open: one compartment holds gold coins, one bars of gold, one diamonds, pearls, and rubies. Half mad with joy, he runs wildly about the rocks, then kneels and prays. He counts a thousand gold ingots, twenty-five thousand old crowns, and handfuls of gems, then sleeps across the mouth of the cave with his gun beside him, a night of joy and terror.

title: The Unknown
summary: Dantès hides the treasure, sells a few gems, buys a yacht, and learns that his father is dead and Mercédès has vanished. Using the name Lord Wilmore, he returns unrecognized to Marseilles, buys his father’s old house, and visits the Catalans.
details: Dantès carefully disguises the cave entrance and, when the smugglers return six days later, pretends he is still lame. At Leghorn (Livorno) he sells four small diamonds to a dealer, then gives Jacopo a brand-new boat and money, explaining that he has just inherited a fortune from an uncle. He sends Jacopo to Marseilles to find out what has become of an old man named Louis Dantès and a young Catalan woman named Mercédès.

At Genoa, Dantès buys a fast little yacht that had been built for an Englishman, paying well over its price, and has the builder fit a secret three-part closet at the head of his bed. He sails alone to Monte Cristo, moves the whole treasure into the hidden closet, and spends a week learning how the boat handles. When Jacopo arrives, the news is grim: old Dantès is dead, and Mercédès has disappeared.

Confident that his face has changed beyond recognition, Dantès sails boldly into Marseilles on an English passport. A sailor from his old ship, the Pharaon, talks with him without recognizing him and is rewarded handsomely for his honesty. Dantès visits his father’s old rooms, now rented by a newly married couple, and weeps where the old man died. He learns that Caderousse, the former tailor downstairs, now keeps an inn near Beaucaire. Under the name on his passport, Lord Wilmore, he buys the house for far more than it is worth, spends an hour in the Catalan village asking about people long dead or gone, gives the family he questioned a new fishing boat, and rides out of Marseilles.

title: The Pont du Gard Inn
summary: Caderousse, now a struggling innkeeper with a sickly wife, is visited by an Italian priest who says Dantès died in prison and left a diamond to be shared among his friends. Caderousse reveals that old Dantès starved to death.
details: Caderousse and his wife, Madeleine, nicknamed La Carconte, keep a failing roadside inn between Beaucaire and Bellegarde; a new canal has carried off their trade. She is pale, shaking with marsh fever, and constantly complaining; he answers that it is God’s will. One scorching noon a priest arrives on horseback, speaking with a strong Italian accent. He studies Caderousse closely and makes sure he is the former tailor of the Allées de Meilhan in Marseilles.

The abbé asks about a young sailor named Dantès. Caderousse claims to have been his close friend and seems genuinely upset to hear that he died a broken man in prison. The abbé explains that a rich fellow prisoner gave Dantès a diamond worth fifty thousand francs, and that Dantès asked for it to be sold and shared among his father, his fiancée Mercédès, and three friends: Caderousse, Danglars, and Fernand. Asked how old Dantès died, Caderousse says the doctors called it a stomach illness, but the truth is he starved. The abbé leaps up, badly shaken.

La Carconte, listening from the stairs, warns her husband to keep quiet, because Fernand and Danglars are now rich and powerful. Caderousse hints that the two were traitors, not friends. When the abbé calmly says he will simply find them and give them their shares, greed wins: Caderousse bolts the door and sits down to tell the whole story, while the priest places himself in the shadows to listen.

title: The Story
summary: Caderousse tells the abbé everything: old Dantès’s slow death, the denunciation written by Danglars and posted by Fernand, Morrel’s near ruin, and how Danglars became a rich baron and Fernand the Count de Morcerf, husband of Mercédès. The abbé gives him the diamond.
details: Once promised secrecy, Caderousse describes old Dantès’s last months: pacing all night, refusing to leave home in case Edmond came back, quietly selling his belongings, and finally, using a doctor’s diet as an excuse, refusing all food until he died nine days later, blessing his son. Mercédès and M. Morrel tried to help; Morrel left a red silk purse that paid the old man’s debts and funeral. Then Caderousse names the culprits: Danglars, driven by ambition, wrote the denunciation with his left hand at La Réserve, and Fernand, driven by love, posted it. Caderousse admits he was there, drunk, and afterwards kept silent out of fear.

Morrel, who pleaded for Dantès again and again, is now nearly ruined, with every hope riding on the Pharaon. Danglars made a fortune supplying the army in Spain, married well, and is now Baron Danglars, a Paris millionaire. Fernand deserted to the enemy with a general in 1815, rose in the army, won the title Count de Morcerf in the Spanish war, served Ali Pasha in Greece, and is now a lieutenant-general with a grand house in Paris.

Mercédès, alone after Edmond vanished and his father died, eventually married Fernand in the very church where she was to have married Edmond. She educated herself, has a son, Albert, and is now a great lady, yet Caderousse believes she is unhappy; she once secretly dropped him a purse. Villefort married Mademoiselle de Saint-Méran and left Marseilles. The abbé gives Caderousse the diamond in exchange for Morrel’s red purse and rides away. La Carconte suspects the stone is fake, so Caderousse rushes off to have it valued at the Beaucaire fair.

title: The Prison Register
summary: Posing as an English clerk of the Roman bank Thomson & French, Dantès buys M. de Boville’s endangered loan to Morrel and, in return, examines the prison records, secretly pocketing Danglars’s denunciation and discovering Villefort’s role in his imprisonment.
details: The day after the visit to Caderousse, a man of about thirty-two with an English manner and accent calls on the mayor of Marseilles. He says he is chief clerk of Thomson & French, a banking house in Rome, and is worried about money lent to Morrel & Son. The mayor, himself a creditor, praises Morrel’s honesty and sends him to M. de Boville, the inspector of prisons, who has two hundred thousand francs, his daughter’s dowry, invested with Morrel. Boville is in despair: Morrel has just told him he cannot pay unless the Pharaon arrives by the 15th.

The Englishman offers to buy the debt at its full value, in cash. The only “commission” he asks is a look at the prison registers: he says he was taught in Rome by an abbé named Faria and wants to know how he died. Boville happily tells the story, including how a dangerous Bonapartist named Edmond Dantès dug a tunnel to Faria’s cell, took the dead man’s place in his burial sack, and was thrown into the sea with a cannonball tied to his feet. Boville roars with laughter, and the Englishman laughs too. Officially, Dantès is dead.

Left alone with the files, the Englishman reads Dantès’s dossier: the accusation, the record of his examination (which never mentions Noirtier), and Morrel’s petition of April 1815, exaggerated on Villefort’s advice while Napoleon ruled and later turned into a weapon against Dantès. A note in Villefort’s handwriting orders strict solitary confinement for an “inveterate Bonapartist.” Unseen, the Englishman slips Danglars’s original denunciation into his pocket, then pays Boville and receives the transfer of the debt.

title: The House of Morrel & Son
summary: The Thomson & French clerk visits the desperate Morrel, who owes 287,500 francs. News comes that the Pharaon has sunk; the stranger grants three months’ delay and tells Julie Morrel to obey a future letter signed “Sinbad the Sailor.”
details: Morrel’s once-bustling firm is almost deserted. Only two employees remain: Emmanuel, a young clerk in love with Morrel’s daughter, and the one-eyed cashier Cocles, whose faith that the firm will always pay is as fixed as his arithmetic. Morrel, now fifty and white-haired, has secretly sold his wife’s and daughter’s jewels to meet last month’s bills. Everything depends on the Pharaon, long overdue from Calcutta.

The Englishman is shown up, passing Morrel’s daughter Julie on the stairs. He reveals that his firm has bought up Morrel’s bills, Boville’s included, worth 287,500 francs, and asks frankly whether Morrel can pay. Morrel admits that if the Pharaon is lost he will have to stop payment. At that moment Julie bursts in weeping: the Pharaon has sunk, though the crew was rescued by another ship. The old sailor Penelon tells of the storm, of Captain Gaumard’s courage, and of three days adrift without food; the Englishman, clearly an expert seaman, comments on the handling of the ship.

Morrel pays the sailors what he can, and they generously offer to wait for the rest. Alone with Morrel, the Englishman, moved to tears, grants three months’ grace, renewing the bills until 5 September at eleven o’clock. Morrel thanks him, privately vowing to pay or die. On the stairs the stranger tells Julie that one day she will receive a letter signed “Sinbad the Sailor,” which she must obey exactly, however strange, and hints that she will marry Emmanuel. Then he asks Penelon for a word in private.

title: The Fifth of September
summary: Facing bankruptcy, Morrel prepares to shoot himself at eleven. At the last moment Julie brings a red purse holding his paid bill and a diamond for her dowry, and a new Pharaon sails in. The unknown benefactor departs, turning now to vengeance.
details: The delay lets Morrel scrape through June, July, and August, paying bills against everyone’s expectations. Captain Gaumard returns, and Morrel notices Penelon, newly dressed and oddly embarrassed, and assumes he has found a new master. Morrel’s last hope, a trip to Paris to ask Danglars, who owes his start in life to Morrel, ends in a humiliating refusal. Julie writes to her brother Maximilian, a principled young army officer nicknamed “the stoic,” to come home, and Madame Morrel sees her husband writing what looks like his will.

On the morning of 5 September, Maximilian arrives and discovers pistols under his father’s coat. Morrel shows him the books: 287,500 francs owed, about 15,000 in hand. Dying, Morrel says, he leaves an honest name; living, he would only be a bankrupt. Maximilian accepts, takes off his epaulets, and promises to live for his mother and sister and to repay every debt, starting with Thomson & French. Morrel waits alone as the clock nears eleven, the pistol in his mouth.

Meanwhile a messenger with an Italian accent hands Julie a letter from “Sinbad the Sailor” telling her to fetch a red silk purse from a fifth-floor room at 15 Allées de Meilhan, Dantès’s father’s old home. She bursts in just in time: the purse, Morrel’s own long-lost one, holds the receipted bill and a huge diamond labelled “Julie’s Dowry.” Then Emmanuel shouts that the Pharaon is entering the harbor: an exact copy of the lost ship, cargo and all, with Gaumard and Penelon aboard. Hidden in the crowd, a man with a black beard blesses Morrel, calls for Jacopo, and boards his yacht, declaring that, having rewarded the good, he will now punish the wicked.

title: Italy: Sinbad the Sailor
summary: In 1838 Franz d’Épinay, on his way to meet Albert de Morcerf for the Roman Carnival, lands on Monte Cristo, where a mysterious host calling himself “Sinbad the Sailor” entertains him in a hidden underground palace and offers him hashish.
details: Years have passed. Early in 1838 two young Parisian aristocrats, Viscount Albert de Morcerf and Baron Franz d’Épinay, plan to see the Carnival in Rome and book rooms with Signor Pastrini at the Hôtel de Londres. While Albert visits Naples, Franz tours Elba and, after poor hunting on Pianosa, accepts his boat captain Gaetano’s suggestion to hunt wild goats on the uninhabited island of Monte Cristo, in spite of grim stories about pirates who sink ships with their crews aboard.

At night they see a fire on the shore. Gaetano swims in to scout and reports Spanish smugglers with two Corsican bandits, men he treats as fellow sailors. Franz is made welcome, and the smugglers’ chief invites him to supper, on condition that he is blindfolded. The sailors say the chief calls himself Sinbad the Sailor, owns a fast Genoese yacht, and lives in a cave more splendid than any palace.

With the blindfold removed, Franz meets a strikingly handsome man of about forty in Tunisian dress, deathly pale, in rooms full of crimson brocade, marble statues, and treasures. Franz takes the name Aladdin for the evening. Ali, a mute Nubian whom Sinbad saved from the Bey of Tunis, serves a lavish supper. Sinbad speaks of vows still to be fulfilled, of dispensing his own secret justice, and of going to Paris one day; when Franz guesses at revenge, his host laughs it off. Then Sinbad offers him hashish, and Franz sinks into a wild, sensual dream in which the statues come to life.

title: The Waking
summary: Franz wakes in a bare grotto to find that Sinbad has sailed away. Unable to find the secret entrance, he leaves the island and travels to Rome, where he joins Albert at Signor Pastrini’s crowded hotel on the eve of Carnival.
details: Franz wakes on a bed of heather in an ordinary-looking grotto, his head clear and the dream of the statues gone. Gaetano passes on Sinbad’s apologies: urgent business has called him to Malaga. Through his telescope Franz sees his host standing on the deck of his yacht, waving farewell, and hears a small gun fired in salute.

Franz spends hours searching the cave walls with a torch and his hunting knife, but finds no trace of the hidden door, only smoke marks left by others who have tried. He notices the yacht heading for Corsica, not Malaga, and Gaetano explains that Sinbad is landing the two Corsican bandits: he is said to fear neither God nor devil and will sail far out of his way to help a hunted man. With nothing more to learn, Franz sails off, and the whole adventure begins to feel like a dream.

After finishing his business in Florence, Franz reaches Rome just before the Carnival, with the streets packed. Signor Pastrini welcomes him and Albert to their small rooms; the rest of the floor has been taken by a very rich gentleman thought to be Sicilian or Maltese. Pastrini warns that carriages and horses are impossible to find, but Albert, sure that a full purse solves everything, goes happily to bed.

title: Roman Bandits
summary: Signor Pastrini warns Franz and Albert about the bandit Luigi Vampa and tells his story: a gifted shepherd who loved Teresa, killed the bandit chief Cucumetto, and took over his band. Franz is startled to hear that Vampa once met a traveller called Sinbad the Sailor.
details: Pastrini can find the friends a carriage only until Sunday, and windows overlooking the Corso are all taken. When Franz plans a moonlight drive outside the city walls to the Colosseum, Pastrini warns them about Luigi Vampa, a young bandit who kills prisoners whose ransom arrives late. Albert scoffs, but Franz wants to hear more; Pastrini knew Vampa as a child and was once captured and freed by him, receiving a fine watch as a gift.

Vampa was a shepherd boy on the Count of San-Felice’s farm, astonishingly quick: he taught himself to read and write, carved wood beautifully, and became a deadly shot. He grew up beside Teresa, a beautiful, vain orphan shepherdess, and they planned to marry. Pastrini also describes the brutal bandit chief Cucumetto, including the story of Carlini, a bandit who stabbed his beloved Rita to save her from the band. Vampa and Teresa once hid Cucumetto from soldiers and refused his gold, though Teresa’s eyes lit up at the sight of it.

At the count’s Carnival ball, Teresa dances with nobles alongside the count’s daughter Carmela, and Vampa burns with jealousy. That night the villa catches fire; an unknown peasant rescues Carmela, and next day Vampa presents Teresa with Carmela’s costume and jewels. While guiding a lost traveller, who gives his name as Sinbad the Sailor, Vampa hears Teresa scream: Cucumetto is carrying her off. Vampa shoots him dead, puts on his clothes, and leads Teresa to the bandits, who make him their captain. Franz, struck by the name Sinbad, decides they will drive to the Colosseum through the city streets.

title: The Colosseum
summary: At the Colosseum Franz overhears a cloaked man, whose voice he knows as Sinbad’s, promise a bandit to save the condemned Peppino. At the opera he sees the same man with a beautiful Greek girl, and next morning the friends call on their neighbour, the Count of Monte Cristo.
details: In the moonlit Colosseum, Franz slips away from the guides and, hidden behind a pillar, watches a cloaked man meet a peasant from the Trastevere district, who drops in through a hole in the roof. Two men are to be executed in two days, the peasant reports: a murderer and Peppino, a shepherd whose only crime was supplying food to the peasant’s band. He plans to rescue Peppino by force; the cloaked man promises instead to buy a pardon, and will signal success by hanging the middle one of three windows he has rented on the Corso with white damask and a red cross. In return the peasant swears absolute obedience. Franz recognizes the voice as Sinbad’s.

Next evening at the Teatro Argentina, Albert, stung at having had no romantic adventures in Italy, gets Franz to introduce him to the Venetian Countess G——. In a box opposite, Franz sees a lovely woman in Greek dress with a motionless man in the shadows behind her. When the man stands, Franz recognizes Sinbad. The countess, shuddering at his pallor, calls him a vampire, “Lord Ruthven himself,” and makes Franz escort her home. Albert later reports that the man spoke modern Greek and was very elegantly dressed.

Back at the hotel, Pastrini announces that the Count of Monte Cristo, who has the rest of their floor, offers them seats in his carriage and at his windows in the Rospoli Palace, and the count’s servant brings his cards. Next morning the posted execution notice names Andrea Rondolo and Peppino, and Franz concludes that the peasant was Luigi Vampa himself. When the friends call on the count, Franz recognizes him as the man from the Colosseum, the theatre, and Monte Cristo.

title: La Mazzolata
summary: The Count of Monte Cristo entertains Franz and Albert, sets out a chilling philosophy of revenge, and takes them to watch the executions. Peppino is pardoned at the scaffold; the murderer Andrea, raging, is clubbed and stabbed to death while the count looks on in triumph.
details: The count greets the friends warmly, gives no sign of knowing Franz, and summons his steward Bertuccio, who looks exactly like the smuggler who led Franz into the cave on Monte Cristo, to confirm his window over the Piazza del Popolo. Reading Franz’s copy of the execution notice, the count remarks that he has heard Peppino may be pardoned.

When the talk turns to punishment, the count says he has seen the tortures of nearly every nation. With sudden hatred in his face, he argues that the guillotine is too quick a pain for someone who has caused years of suffering, such as destroying a man’s father, mother, or betrothed, and that a duel is no true revenge either; slow, deep torment should be repaid in kind, “an eye for an eye.” Albert simply enjoys the breakfast and the count’s cigars, but Franz notices that the count barely eats and keeps looking intently at Albert. The count says he will visit Paris soon, and Albert promises to return his hospitality there.

On the way, Franz sees the count’s three windows on the Corso: two hung with yellow damask and the middle one white with a red cross. The count has kept his promise. From their window they watch the procession of penitents, the executioner with his heavy mallet, and the two prisoners. As Peppino reaches the scaffold, a pardon is read out. Andrea, the murderer, goes berserk, screaming that Peppino must die with him, and the count laughs bitterly at this proof of human nature. Andrea is struck down with the mallet and his throat is cut. Franz half faints and Albert clings to the curtains, while the count stands upright “like the Avenging Angel.”

title: The Carnival at Rome
summary: The Carnival begins. Albert flirts with a masked peasant woman who throws him violets and sends him a note arranging a meeting. The count lends the friends his carriage and box but remains an enigma to Franz. On the last night Albert vanishes with his mysterious beauty.
details: As Franz recovers, the count is already changing into costume; Peppino, he says, slipped away in the crowd. The friends throw themselves into the Corso’s mad battle of confetti and flowers in the count’s carriage. The count leaves them at the Rospoli Palace, where Franz imagines that the figure in a blue domino (a hooded masquerade cloak) at the window is the Greek girl. Albert catches the eye of a woman in a carriage full of Roman peasants, who throws him a bunch of violets.

At the theatre Franz tells the Countess G—— that the count is a Tuscan count named after the island he bought, and she decides her vampire is just an eccentric millionaire. Over the next days the count lends the friends his carriage freely and impresses them with his knowledge of literature, painting, and chemistry. Albert’s flirtation grows: the woman lifts her mask and is charming, and Albert, sure she is a noblewoman, writes to her. Her elegant reply tells him to follow the peasant who snatches his candle at the church of San Giacomo on Tuesday evening. Franz, meanwhile, is received by Pope Gregory XVI.

To Franz the count is a puzzle out of Byron: he must know Franz recognizes him, yet he never mentions their earlier meetings. Franz admires him but does not want to be in Paris when he arrives there. On Tuesday, the last day, after the horse races, the Corso blazes with thousands of moccoletti, small candles that everyone tries to blow out. At seven, Albert, dressed as a harlequin with rose ribbons, has his candle snatched by a masked peasant woman and disappears with her toward the Via Macello. Then the bell sounds, every light goes out, and the Carnival is over.

title: The Catacombs of Saint Sebastian
summary: A ransom note reveals that Luigi Vampa has kidnapped Albert. Franz turns to the count, who, guided by Peppino, takes him to the bandits’ lair in the catacombs, where Vampa apologizes and frees Albert at once. Franz notices the count shudder as he shakes Albert’s hand.
details: Albert does not come back. At the Duke of Bracciano’s ball Franz learns that a man has brought a letter from Albert. It asks for four thousand piastres; beneath it, a note signed Luigi Vampa says that if the money is not paid by six in the morning, Albert will die at seven. Franz is several hundred piastres short and goes to the count, who offers his gold freely. Franz suggests a better way: the count saved Peppino’s life, so surely Vampa will release Albert for him.

The count calls up the cloaked messenger, who turns out to be Peppino and falls to his knees in gratitude. He explains the trap: Vampa himself drove the peasants’ carriage, Teresa flirted with Albert with his consent, and the “peasant girl” at San Giacomo was Beppo, a fifteen-year-old boy, who led Albert into an ambush outside the walls. Ali, the mute servant from Monte Cristo, drives the count, Franz, and Peppino out along the Appian Way to the catacombs of Saint Sebastian.

Through dark tunnels they reach a burial chamber where Vampa sits reading among twenty bandits. When the guns are raised, the count calmly reproaches Vampa for breaking their agreement that the count’s friends would be respected. Vampa, mortified, threatens his own men and apologizes. Albert is found sound asleep, dreaming of a dance with the Countess G——, and accepts his release with perfect coolness, thanking the count and lighting his cigar from Vampa’s torch. Vampa tells Franz his favorite book is Caesar’s Commentaries. By two o’clock Albert is dancing at the ball, while Franz wonders why the count shuddered when he had to take Albert’s hand.
